stories.title: US plans $725 million payment towards its large UN debt
stories.summary: WASHINGTON/GENEVA, Aug 21 - The Trump administration has started the process to transfer $725 million to the United Nations, a congressional notification seen by Reuters showed, a move aid experts said was a welcome step towards paying billions in dues owed. There was no immediate response from Washington to questions about the reasons for the payment from an administration which has slashed funding to many U.N. agencies and blasted the global body for not living up to its potential. The money - mentioned in an August 4 State Department notification letter to Congress that has not been reported - is set to go through before an expected speech by U.S. President Donald Trump to the U.N. General Assembly in New York next month. U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said this year that the U.N. faced "imminent financial collapse" due to unpaid contributions from member states, and the global body has brought in large budget cuts. The $725 million would be less than 20% of the more than $4 billion that the U.N. said in May it was owed by the United States — though Washington has said that total figure is much lower and that it has made some payments. Eugene Chen, a former U.N. official, told Reuters such a transfer would help pay U.N. salaries for a period, but might not cover them all. "It keeps the ship afloat a little longer," he said. "If the U.S. does not make further payments it will likely lose its voting rights in January," he added. Under article 19 of the U.N. Charter, a member state loses its voting rights in the General Assembly if its arrears exceed two years in annual fees, although grace periods are possible. A significant transfer now could avert the need for immediate spending cuts, Ronny Patz, an expert in U.N. finance with German think tank IDOS, said. The U.S. is the biggest contributor to the U.N. budget, but under the Trump administration it has refused to make mandatory payments to regular and peacekeeping budgets, and has slashed voluntary funding to U.N. agencies with their own budgets. Washington has also withdrawn from dozens of U.N. and other international agencies.

stories.title: China-Africa media cooperation: Building skills for the AI era
stories.summary: Africa and China are deepening cooperation in the media sector as digital transformation and artificial intelligence reshape how news and content are produced. The 7th Forum on China-Africa Media Cooperation opened in Beijing under the theme “Share Development Opportunities, Shape the Audio-Visual Future,” bringing together media leaders and professionals from across Africa and China. For Gregoire Ndjaka, CEO and Director General of the African Union of Broadcasting, media cooperation goes beyond technology — it is also a bridge between cultures. He highlighted growing opportunities for African journalists to receive training in China and across Africa, including recent programmes focused on using artificial intelligence to produce content. Ndjaka stressed that Africa must not simply consume AI technologies, but develop the skills to understand, adapt and use them for its own development. For him, AI represents a potential shortcut to accelerating Africa’s development — provided African media professionals are equipped to master the technology. As the media landscape becomes increasingly digital and intelligent, the message from Beijing is clear: skills, technology and knowledge-sharing will be central to Africa’s ability to shape its own digital future.

stories.title: Too early to discuss reduction in threat of merchant ship seizures — Kremlin
stories.summary: Dmitry Peskov commented on whether the Kremlin has observed a decline in threats to maritime trade
article_sentences: MOSCOW, August 21.
It is premature to discuss the impact of Russia’s warning of a tit-for-tat response to Western attempts to seize merchant vessels, Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov told TASS.
"It’s too early to raise that question," he said in response to a question about whether the Kremlin has observed a decline in threats to maritime trade.

On August 12, while addressing the Pacific Fleet exercises, Russian President Vladimir Putin stated that Moscow would retaliate against attempts by several Western countries to seize its merchant vessels.
He also emphasized that this would occur not only in the waters where such raids are planned but also wherever Russia deems appropriate.
